case_name: Selim v Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner)
text:
Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Selim
v Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner), 2016 ABQB 562

Date:
20161006

Docket:
1603 06962

Registry:
Edmonton

Between:

Yaser Khedr Selim

Plaintiff

- and -

Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner

of Alberta (FOIP)

Defendant

_______________________________________________________

Memorandum of Decision

of the

Honourable
Madam Justice

J.B. Veit

_______________________________________________________

Summary

[
1
]

Mr. Selim “appeals” the decision of the
Information and Privacy Commissioner who refused to conduct an inquiry into records
of the Calgary Police Service relating to a female model known as JC . This
court hears Mr. Selim’s application as one for judicial review of the Commissioner’s
decision.

[
2
]

A Calgary Police Service detective initiated
contact with Mr. Selim about Mr. Selim’s attempts to locate a female model
known as JC. The detective and Mr. Selim then exchanged a large number of
emails and telephone conversations over a period of 7 months in 2013. During
that time, the detective suggested that Mr. Selim write a letter to JC and the
detective would deliver it to JC. Subsequently Mr. Selim received a response letter,
purportedly from JC, postmarked from Juneau, Alaska where the detective had
told Mr. Selim that JC currently resided with her family. When, in November
2013, the detective refused any continued contact with Mr. Selim, the latter
made a FOIP request to the Calgary Police Service for information about JC.
CPS responded to Mr. Selim that it had no records on JC. Mr. Selim then
requested a review by the Information and Privacy Commissioner of the CPS
response. The Commissioner authorized a Commission staff member to conduct an
investigation and to attempt to settle the dispute. The attempt at settlement
was not successful. Invoking s. 69 of the
Freedom of Information and
Protection of Privacy Act,
Mr. Selim then requested the Commissioner to
conduct an inquiry into his original request for records. On July 20, 2015, the
Commissioner asked the CPS to submit to it a sworn document by no later than
August 19, 2015, setting out the specific steps that by CPS to identify and
locate records responsive to Mr. Selim’s access request. On August 18, 2015,
CPS submitted a declaration to the effect that it had made inquiries of the
detective in question who had asserted that all communications had been
conducted only in a personal capacity, that no police records existed relative
to JC and that all information the detective had provided to Mr. Selim was “to attempt
to assuage a person suffering from delusional thinking”.  CPS did not provide
to the Commissioner any information about the fabricated letter. After
considering the declaration received from CPS, in January 2016, the
Commissioner informed Mr. Selim that she relied on the declaration from CPS,
that the detective had never been in contact with anyone having the initials JC
and so there could be no CPS records relating to JC. The Commissioner therefore
refused to conduct an inquiry into the existence of records relating to JC, and
closed the file. Mr. Selim now asks for judicial review of the Commissioner’s
decision.

[
3
]

The application for judicial review is
dismissed: the Commissioner’s decision was reasonable.

[
4
]

The applicable standard of review is
reasonableness: that standard has been adopted in similar situations and is
appropriate where, as here, the Commissioner has a statutory discretion to
order an inquiry.

[
5
]

Even though the Commissioner did not receive
information about all of the communications between the CPS and Mr. Selim, and
even though, arguably, the evidence about those communications does not meet
the requirements of the
Alberta Evidence Act –
it may be that the
provisions of that Act relating to affirmations should be reviewed by the
Legislature -  and even though the evidence on which the Commissioner relied
was not independent from the public body whose records were being sought, the
Commissioner was entitled to conclude that there were no CPS records relating
to JC:

-  evidence of the conduct of the
CPS detective that was not presented to the Commissioner was of the same type
as the evidence which was presented and the explanation of the detective that
he had lied to Mr. Selim throughout applies equally to the unpresented
evidence;

-  the deposition from the employee
of the Calgary Police Service was obviously intended to be a legally binding
statement and one which was to have the same effect in relation to perjury as a
statement given under oath;

-  the evidence relied on by the
Commissioner was not independent from CPS and therefore did not advance the
objective set out in s. 2(e) of FOIPPA, but the evidence presented included Mr.
Selim’s communications with CPS from which the context of the relationship
could be discerned;

-   the situation outlined in Mr.
Selim’s own communications was of a matter  having nothing to do with any
Canadian police investigation into any alleged criminal behaviour. Objectively,
relying on Mr. Selim’s own evidence, there was no reason for the CPS to open a
file;

-  the detective made a voluntary  statement
against interest, acknowledging that he had abused his position as a police
officer in order to advance a personal cause, and had, in doing so, repeatedly
and consistently lied to Mr. Selim. As we know from criminal process,
statements against interest are likely to be reliable.

Cases and authority cited

[
6
]

By the Commissioner
:
Carter v Information and Privacy Commissioner
September 9,
2011, Aon No. 1001-17312

[
7
]

By the CPS
: Order
F2015-35
, University of Calgary
, Office of the Information and Privacy
Commissioner, Case File Number F7544

[
8
]

By the court
:
Ontario
(Public Safety and Security) v. Criminal Lawyers' Association

2010
SCC 23
;
Alberta Teachers' Association v. Alberta (Information and Privacy
Commissioner)

2011 ABQB 19
;
R. v Hatchard

2016 BCCA 134
.

1.         Background

a)
Factual

[
9
]

Mr. Selim is a middle-aged man who was born
outside of Canada. He was scammed out of $2,000.00 by con men who used
photographs of women as bait. Mr. Selim came to believe that the woman whose photograph
was used to con him was herself a victim. Mr. Selim became obsessed with that
woman, known only by the initials JC.

[
10
]

The chronology of Mr. Selim’s interaction with
the Calgary Police Service is outlined in the affidavit of the CPS detective who
dealt with him. This affidavit was presented to the court at the court’s
request for additional information about material which had not been seen by
the Commissioner.

In May
2013 a friend of mine who lives in Hawaii contacted me because she and her employees
at the modeling agency she ran were being inundated with telephone calls and
emails from Mr. Yaser Selim. She advised me that Mr. Selim was continually
contacting and harassing the agency inquiring about an individual by the name
of JC whose picture was on the modelling website.

As a
favour to my friend, I contacted Mr. Selim to discuss his actions as they
related to the modelling agency in Hawaii. I tried to explain to him what
criminal harassment was and that he needed to stop contacting the agency in
Hawaii.

My friend from
the modelling agency advised me that JC had not been with the agency for over 8
years and that they had no contact information for her. I believe that
information was true and I passed that information on to Mr. Selim in the hopes
that it would convince him not to contact the agency further.

I did not
open a police investigation file or initiate any formal CPS documentation.

,,,

In an
attempt to dissuade Mr. Selim from pursuing JC I advised Mr. Selim that JC had
moved to Alaska where she lived happily with her family. I picked Alaska
because I wanted to give Mr. Selim the impression that JC had attempted to
withdraw to a remote place and live quietly with her family. This information
was fabricated by me in an attempt to cause Mr. Selim to lose interest in JC.

. . .

Mr. Selim
provided me a letter to JC and I fabricated a response that advised Mr. Selim
that JC was happily married and could not reciprocate Mr. Selim’s affections. I
tried to make the letter convincing, again with the intention that it would
cause Mr. Selim to lose interest in JC.

. . .

I did not
consider at the time the depth of the deception I was engaged in and the
potential negative consequences it could have.

. . .

An
acquaintance of mine was going to Alaska on a cruise. I provided the letter
that I had drafted pretending to be JC to my acquaintance who agreed to mail it
for me. That is why the letter to Mr. Selim has a postmark from Juneau Alaska.

.

I
understand now that my actions in deceiving Mr. Selim caused him to become
convinced that the Calgary Police Service had records that included information
about how to contact [J.C.] There are no such records.

[
11
]

Because there were a number of telephone
conversations between the detective and Mr. Selim, and because all of Mr.
Selim’s written communications with the detective were not retained, it is not
possible to have a complete outline of the relationship between the two.
However, the following might be noted:

-           from the outset, i.e.
May 8, 2013, Mr. Selim demonstrated a tendency to bombard the detective with
short bursts of messages;

-           the detective’s May 9,
2013 email to Mr. Selim used language such as, “investigation completed”,
“update on your file”, “completed my preliminary investigation and can now
report to you”;

-           on May 13, 2013, the
detective asks Mr. Selim to provide his full name, age and birth date so that
the detective can “update my records associated with this investigation”;

-           on May 23, 2013, the
detective writes to Mr. Selim under the heading “JC and Phase 2 of the
Investigation”;

-           on July 30, 2013, after
having told Mr. Selim that he will take no further telephone calls from him, the
detective writes to Mr. Selim, “I will still prepare and forward the transcript
of my conversation with JC . . . taking no further action”;

-           on August 7, 2013, the
detective sent to Mr. Selim some photos which he described as “possibly being
more photos of JC”;

-           on August 16, 2013, the
detective asks Mr. Selim for his mailing address so that JC can write to Mr.
Selim;

-           on September 19, 2013,
the detective tells Mr. Selim “I will phone [JC] if we haven’t heard anything
by next Thursday”;

-           on September 22, 2013,
the detective writes to Mr. Selim: “I look forward to discussing Tagged matter
with you next week”;

-           on September 24, 2013,
the detective writes to Mr. Selim about the letter Mr. Selim received from
purportedly JC, but in reality one which the detective had fabricated;

-           on September 25, 2013,
stating that he had received 27 emails from Mr. Selim since the previous day,
the detective writes to Mr. Selim that their “work together is finished”;

-           on November 14, 2013,
the detective writes to Mr. Selim, “I will never communicate with JC again”.

[
12
]

All of the detective’s written communications
with Mr. Selim issued from the CPS website, with the CPS insignia.

[
13
]

In January 2014, Mr. Selim made a FOIP request
to the Calgary Police Service with respect to records from someone named JC.
In February 2014, CPS responded to Mr. Selim stating that it had asked the
detective for records and the detective had answered that there were no records
and that CPS was therefore closing its file.

[
14
]

In that initial investigation by CPS, the
detective told CPS staff:

. . . I
did not conduct an investigation. I was using official sounding language to
attempt to assuage a person suffering from delusional thinking. My goal was to
have [Mr. Selim] cease obsessing about this person. The details I shared with
him were not factual personal information and were crafted to attempt to cause
him to give up his obsession . . .

[
15
]

In June 2014, Mr. Selim asked the Commissioner
for a review of the CPS position. In August 2014, the Commissioner authorized
one of its staff members to “investigate and try to settle this matter”. As
apparently is its practice when this step is taken, the Commissioner does not
receive a copy of any investigation report and obviously does not receive
information about the attempts at a settlement other than the information about
whether the attempt was successful or not successful. In this case, since the
attempt at settlement was not successful, Mr. Selim was presumably told that
the Commissioner’s review was complete. Because the Commissioner does not
receive either a copy of the investigation or of the result of the settlement
process, none of that information is contained in the Commissioner’s Record of
Proceedings, or return, on the judicial review application.

[
16
]

In February, 2015, being dissatisfied with the
review, Mr. Selim asked the Commissioner for an inquiry. As is apparently its
practice, the office of the Commissioner then asked CPS “to provide a sworn
statement about the search it conducted” by August 19, 2015. On August 18,
2015, CPS provided an affidavit affirmed by a senior disclosure analyst and
civilian member of the Calgary Police Service who met with the detective in
question on August 18, 2015 and who was informed by the detective that:

-           he “does not know who
JC is, nor does he have any additional information regarding JC”; -          he
had communicated by email with Mr. Selim “but always in his personal capacity”;

-           “any information that
appears to be about JC such as her marital status, or place of residence was
fabricated in an attempt to encourage [Mr. Selim] to move on and stop trying to
pursue JC”.

[
17
]

The CPS did not provide to the Commissioner
information about the detective’s proposing that he receive from Mr. Selim a
letter addressed to JC and thereafter misleading Mr. Selim about the delivery
of that letter, or about the fabrication by the detective of a purported
response letter from JC to Mr. Selim, or about the fact that the detective
arranged for the fabricated letter to be mailed from Juneau, Alaska to make his
deception appear more realistic. The CPS did not make it clear to the
Commissioner that all of the written correspondence between the detective and
Mr. Selim was on a Calgary Police Service computer, using a CPS address and CPS
insignia. Nor did the CPS provide to the Commissioner information about the
extensive telephone communications between Mr. Selim and the detective.

[
18
]

On January 25, 2016, or two years after Mr.
Selim’s FOIP request, the Commissioner provided the following decision to Mr.
Selim concerning his request for an inquiry:

My
decision

It appears
that as a result of interactions between [Mr. Selim] and [the detective], [Mr.
Selim] believed that [the detective] had been in contact with JC and was
seeking records about that contact. As is evident from the affidavit of the
Senior Disclosure Analyst, [the detective] had never been in contact with
anyone having the initials “JC”, and so there could be no records about JC that
[Mr. Selim} requested.

Based on
the affidavit, I find that the CPS conducted an adequate search for records
that [Mr. Selim] requested. I am therefore refusing to conduct an inquiry on
that issue and have closed [the file].

b)
Legislative

[
19
]

The
Freedom of Information and Protection of
Privacy Act
contains the following provisions:

Division
1

Reviews
by the Commissioner

Right
to ask for a review

65(1)  A
person who makes a request to the head of a public body for access to a record
or for correction of personal information may ask the Commissioner to review
any decision, act or failure to act of the head that relates to the request.

. . .

Mediation
may be authorized

68   The
Commissioner may authorize a mediator to investigate and try to settle any
matter that is the subject of a request for a review.

Inquiry
by Commissioner

69(1)
Unless section 70 applies, if a matter is not settled under section 68, the
Commissioner must conduct an inquiry and may decide all questions of fact and
law arising in the course of the inquiry.

(2)  An
inquiry under subsection (1) may be conducted in private.

(3)  The
person who asked for the review, the head of the public body concerned and any
other person given a copy of the request for the review must be given an
opportunity to make representations to the Commissioner during the inquiry, but
no one is entitled to be present during, to have access to or to comment on
representations made to the Commissioner by another person.

(4)  The
Commissioner may decide whether the representations are to be made orally or in
writing.

(5)  The
person who asked for the review, the head of the public body concerned and any
other person given a copy of the request for the review may be represented at
the inquiry by counsel or an agent.

(6)  An
inquiry under this section must be completed within 90 days after receiving the
request for the review unless the Commissioner

(a)
notifies the person who asked for the review, the head of the public body
concerned and any other person given a copy of the request for the review that
the Commissioner is extending that period, and

(b)
provides an anticipated date for the completion of the review.

Refusal to conduct
an inquiry

70 The
Commissioner may refuse to conduct an inquiry pursuant to section 69 if in the
opinion of the Commissioner

(a) the
subject-matter of a request for a review under section 65 has been dealt with
in an order or investigation report of the Commissioner, or

(b) the
circumstances warrant refusing to conduct an inquiry.

[
20
]

The
Alberta Evidence Act
contains the
following provisions relating to oaths and affirmations:

Oaths
and Affirmations

Form,
etc., of oath

14(1)
When an oath may lawfully be administered to a person

(a)    as
a witness or as a deponent in an action,

(b)    on
appointment to an office or employment,

(c)    on
any occasion whatever,

that
person is bound by the oath administered if it has been administered in a form
and with any ceremonies that the person may declare to be binding.

(2)  When
an oath is duly administered and taken, the fact that the person to whom it was
administered has at the time of taking the oath no religious belief does not
for any purpose affect the validity of the oath.

Administration
of oath

15(1)  An
oath may be administered in the form and manner following:

The person taking the oath shall hold the Bible or New Testament, or Old
Testament in the case of an adherent of the Jewish religion, in the person’s
uplifted hand and the officer administering the oath shall say:  “You swear
that the evidence you give as touching the matters in question in this action
or matter shall be the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.  So
help you God”, to which the person being sworn shall say “I do” or give his or
her assent to it in a manner satisfactory to the court or to the officer
administering the oath.

2)
Without in any way limiting or restricting the manner in which an oath may be
administered, the oath may be taken or sworn on any one of the 4 Gospels.

Scottish
oath

16   If a
person to whom an oath is to be administered desires to swear with uplifted
hand in the form and manner in which an oath is usually administered in
Scotland the person shall be permitted to do so, and the oath shall be
administered to the person in that form and manner without further question.

Affirmation,
etc., instead of oath

17(1)  If,
in an action or on an occasion when an oath is required or permitted, a person
called as a witness, or required or desiring to give evidence or to make an
affidavit or deposition, objects to taking an oath or is objected to as
incompetent to take an oath, if the presiding judge or the person qualified to
take affidavits or depositions is satisfied that the witness or deponent
objects to being sworn

(a)
from conscientious scruples,

(b)
on the ground of the religious belief of the witness or deponent, or

(c)
on the ground that the taking of an oath would have no binding effect on the
conscience of the witness or deponent,

the
witness or deponent may make an affirmation and declaration instead of taking
an oath.

(2)  The
affirmation and declaration of that person is of the same force and effect as
if that person had taken an oath in the usual form.

(3)  When
the evidence is in the form of an affidavit or written deposition, the person
before whom it is taken shall certify that the deponent satisfied the person
that the deponent was a person entitled to affirm.

Statutory
declaration

18   Any
person authorized by law to administer oaths or to take affidavits in any
matter may receive the solemn declaration of any person making it before the
authorized person, in the following form, in attestation of the execution of
any writing, deed or instrument or of the truth of any fact or of any account
rendered in writing:

I,           , solemnly declare that (state the fact or facts declared to), and
I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and
knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath.

Declared before me at                    this __ day of ____ , 20  .

2.         The standard of
review of the Commissioner’s decision is reasonableness

[
21
]

The decision about whether or not an inquiry
will be undertaken is deep within the core of the Commissioner’s rights and
responsibilities. The statute itself gives to the Commissioner discretion to
refuse to conduct an inquiry. As much case law has decided, the appropriate
standard of review in such situations is reasonableness: see, for example,
Criminal
Lawyers’ Association
at para.
70
.

3.         The Commissioner’s refusal
to conduct an inquiry is not unreasonable

a)         General
principles of interpretation of the Commissioner’s obligation to hold an
inquiry

[
22
]

In deciding whether the Commissioner’s decision
not to hold an inquiry was reasonable, I begin with a purposive interpretation
of
the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act.
The Act
itself sets out its objectives:

Purposes
of this Act

2   The
purposes of this Act are

(a)    to
allow any person a right of access to the records in the custody or under the
control of a public body subject to limited and specific exceptions as set out
in this Act,

. . .

(e)    to
provide for independent reviews of decisions made by public bodies under this
Act and the resolution of complaints under this Act.

[
23
]

In this case, Mr. Selim was seeking information
which he believed was contained in records of the Calgary Police Service. We
are therefore dealing with purpose 2(a) of the statute.

[
24
]

As the Supreme Court of Canada succinctly put it
in
Criminal Lawyers’ Association
:

Access to
information in the hands of public institutions can increase transparency in
government, contribute to an informed public, and enhance an open and
democratic society.

[
25
]

With this background informing the
interpretation of the statute, we better understand my colleague Graesser J.’s
conclusion, in
Alberta Teachers’ Association
, that the statute
establishes a default position on the holding of inquiries, which is that the
Commissioner must hold an inquiry:

114.     .
. . Under FOIPPA, if the matter has not been resolved at the mediation stage,
the Commissioner
must hold a hearing
:

115     It
seems clear that the default position under FOIPPA is that there must be an
inquiry.

[Emphasis
in original]

[
26
]

However, as Graesser J. goes on to state:

The
Commissioner has a discretion to not hold an inquiry and an exercise of such
discretion would surely have to be explained because the Commissioner would
essentially be making a final decision.

[
27
]

I agree with Graesser J.’s interpretation of the
statute.

[
28
]

The situation here is not one where the public
body, the Calgary Police Service, has records but invokes some basis on which
it should not be required to produce the records. The CPS senior disclosure
analyst who provided evidence to the Commissioner included the following
paragraph in her statutory declaration:

Even if
the Calgary Police Service did have [information about JC], which it does not,
it could not be supplied to [Mr. Selim]. Based on my training and experience
asa Senior Disclousre Analyst and my review of the FOIPP Act, I am of the view
that the information requested by [Mr. Selim] would be an unreasonable
violation of the personal privacy of the third party JC and therefore we would
be required to refuse disclosure of that information pursuant to s. 17(1) of
the FOIPP Act.

[
29
]

If the situation had been that there were
records, but the CPS refused to provide them to Mr. Selim, the Commissioner
would presumably have had to consider the appropriateness of the public body’s
refusal. However, on the facts of this case, that second level of potential
consideration has no application. Rather, this is a situation where the CPS,
and subsequently the Commissioner herself, have concluded that there are no
records to be produced.

b)         The
Commissioner gave reasons for refusing to open an inquiry

[
30
]

The Commissioner did, as she was required to do,
give reasons for not holding an inquiry.

[
31
]

Although the reasons given were somewhat terse,
being limited to relying on an affidavit prepared by the very agency whose
records were being sought, the reasons were sufficient to meet the obligation
to explain to Mr. Selim why an inquiry was refused.

c)
The
reasons given by the Commissioner were reasonable

[
32
]

In assessing whether the Commissioner’s decision
not to open an inquiry was reasonable, I must consider the evidence on which
the Commissioner relied.

(i)
The
evidence presented to the Commissioner may not have technically met the
requirements of the Alberta Evidence Act

[
33
]

The Commissioner asked the CPS to produce an
affidavit. Although there is some language in some cases which suggests that an
affidavit is a deposition made under oath or solemn declaration, the
traditional meaning of affidavit is a deposition taken under oath: see, for
example,
Black’s Law Dictionary
.

[
34
]

Unsurprisingly, the
Alberta Evidence Act
states
that, where a statement under oath is required, a person may, instead, make an
affirmation or declaration. However, as can be seen from s. 17(3) and s. 18 of
that Act, there are formalities which must be taken to make the affirmation as
legally binding as would be an oath.

[
35
]

The necessity of presenting evidence pursuant to
rigorous legislated standards is, obviously, important, not only because of the
obligation to follow the statutory requirements but also to ensure the reliability
of the evidence in the context that the deponent understands that a false
affirmation will make the deponent liable to prosecution for perjury. The
provisions of the
Canada Evidence Act
which relate to the latter are ss.
14 and 15.

[
36
]

Here, there is no certification from the person
who received the affirmation that the senior disclosure analyst in question was
entitled to affirm. Nor was the declaration taken from the deponent in the
correct way, i.e. as a statutory declaration in which the deponent not only
declares that the facts in the deposition are true, but solemnly declares it,
and acknowledges that the declaration is of the same effect as if made under
oath – i.e. that the deponent is subject to the prohibition against perjury.

[
37
]

Nonetheless, the way in which the deposition of
the senior disclosure analyst was taken demonstrates an intention to make a
solemn declaration for which she could be charged with perjury if it was false and
the Commissioner was entitled to treat it as such.

[
38
]

I pause to observe that it may be timely for the
Legislature to reassess the statutory requirements for affirmations and
declarations.

(ii)
Although
the Commissioner relied on evidence prepared by the very public body whose
records were being sought, and therefore on evidence that was not independent, the
Commissioner was entitled to rely on that evidence

[
39
]

It is surprising that, even though the
Commissioner authorized a review of CPS position, and a review was presumably
conducted, the Commissioner herself never received the results of that review.

[
40
]

One can certainly understand why the
Commissioner does not receive any report on attempted settlement other,
presumably, than a statement to the effect that the settlement efforts were
successful or unsuccessful: it is long settled law that, for obvious policy
reasons, attempts at settlement are privileged. However, the fact that the
content of the settlement efforts is privileged does not explain why the
Commissioner does not receive a report from the senior information and privacy
manager whom she authorized to investigate the matter of the Selim complaint.

[
41
]

One of the legislated objectives of FOIPPA is
precisely to “provide for
independent
reviews of decisions”. The
Commissioner’s staff appears to be the ideal independent investigator, but that
independent investigation is never provided to the Commissioner. Instead, when
the review step is concluded without having given the person who made the
original request satisfaction, the Commissioner then goes to the public body
whose own records are being sought for evidence that an adequate search was
conducted.

(iii)
The
evidence provided to the Commissioner included evidence from Mr. Selim and the
evidence from the latter discloses that there was no Canadian crime to
investigate and no reason for the CPS to open a file

[
42
]

Mr. Selim knew, from the outset, that the
detective with whom he was dealing was attached to the homicide unit and that
the detective was not in the process of investigating a homicide.

[
43
]

Unfortunately, we do not have a record of the
detective’s first communication with Mr. Selim. However, Mr. Selim’s own
correspondence makes it abundantly clear that he understood that the detective
was not investigating a crime; all the detective was allegedly doing was trying
to help Mr. Selim contact a woman. Helping someone to contact someone else is
obviously not a police matter. Mr. Selim should then have realized that it
while it was possible that the detective had some information about the woman
JC, there would be no reason to have a police file or record relating to JC.

(iv)
The
evidence provided to the Commissioner included evidence from the detective in
which he acknowledged improper behaviour on his own part

[
44
]

Part of the evidence that was before the
Commissioner was evidence from the detective who attempted to justify his
conduct. At the same time, however, the detective made many admissions against
interest: he had embarked on this charade as a favour to a friend, i.e. he had
abused his authority as a police officer to advance the interest of a friend;
he admitted having lied repeatedly, consistently and deliberately over a long
period of time to Mr. Selim and to having organized a relatively elaborate ruse
to deceive Mr. Selim. The law, particularly the criminal law, has long
recognized that individuals who make statements against their own interest are,
more likely than not, making statements which can be relied on: see, for
example,
Hatchard
. Case law establishes that the principle
applies to civil procedure as well.

[
45
]

In the result, having considered all of the
material before me, for the reasons outline above, I have concluded that the
Commissioner’s decision not to open an inquiry was reasonable and the
application for judicial review is dismissed.

4.         Costs

[
46
]

I can understand that Mr. Selim might find the
conclusion that CPS have no records relating to JC hard to accept: he has been repeatedly
and consistently lied to by a Calgary police detective and been made subject to
a rather elaborate deception. Because of that conduct, even though Mr. Selim
has not been successful in his application for judicial review, he will not pay
costs to either the CPS or the Commissioner.
